articles.title: Mechanistic Insights Into Long Covid: Viral Persistence, Immune Dysregulation, and Multi-Organ Dysfunction.
articles.snippet: Gupta G, Buonsenso D, Wood J, Mohandas S, Warburton D | Comprehensive Physiology | 2025-Jun | Journal Article; Review
articles.full_summary: This review synthesizes current data on viral persistence, immune dysregulation, and metabolic disturbances as mechanisms driving Long COVID pathogenesis and explores potential therapeutic strategies.
articles.key_finding: Current literature suggests that the mechanisms causing Long Covid involve viral persistence, immune dysregulation, systemic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and metabolic disturbances.

articles.title: Emerging trends in post-COVID immune dysregulation: a narrative review.

articles.full_summary: This narrative review synthesizes findings on immunological assessments in Long COVID patients, highlighting persistent immune dysregulation, autoimmunity, and vascular perturbations, and also mentions viral persistence.
articles.key_finding: Long COVID is characterized by persistent low-grade inflammation, T- and B-cell dysregulation, and prolonged adaptive immune activation. Viral persistence and early immune biomarkers predict long COVID development.

articles.title: Long COVID: A proposed hypothesis-driven model of viral persistence for the pathophysiology of the syndrome.

articles.key_finding: In this model of the long COVID syndrome, the persistence of SARS-CoV-2 is hypothesized to trigger a dysregulated immune system with subsequent heightened release of proinflammatory cytokines that lead to chronic low-grade inflammation and multiorgan symptomatology.

articles.population: 24 participants after acute SARS-CoV-2 infection (with and without continuing symptoms), and a subset of five participants with LC symptoms

articles.title: Peripheral immune progression to long COVID is associated with mitochondrial gene transcription: A meta-analysis.

response.global_summary:
The pathophysiology of Long COVID, also known as post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC), is complex and is largely understood to involve both viral persistence and immune dysregulation [0][1][4][7][13][14][19]. These two mechanisms are often seen as interconnected, with viral persistence potentially triggering or sustaining a dysregulated immune response [2][6][24].

Evidence for viral persistence includes the detection of SARS-CoV-2 components in tissues long after acute infection. A cohort study identified intracellular SARS-CoV-2 spike protein-encoding RNA in rectosigmoid lamina propria tissue in all five participants with Long COVID symptoms up to **676 days** after initial infection [3]. Another cross-sectional study in China found that the detection of viral RNA in recovered patients was significantly associated with the development of Long COVID symptoms, with an **odds ratio of 5.17** (95% CI 2.64-10.13, p<0.0001) [23]. Viral RNA or antigens have been reported to persist in various organs [6][11][24], and one preclinical study detected SARS-CoV-2 S1 protein in CD16+ monocytes in patients with severe COVID-19 and PASC up to **15 months** post-infection [16]. The persistence of viral reactivation, including Anelloviridae, has also been associated with Long COVID [26]. These persistent viral reservoirs are hypothesized to drive chronic inflammation and contribute to multi-organ damage [24].

Immune dysregulation is also widely recognized as a central mechanism [0][1][4][7][14][15][18][19]. This includes persistent low-grade inflammation [1][2][22], T- and B-cell dysregulation [1][15], and prolonged adaptive immune activation [1]. Specific immune profiles observed in Long COVID patients include increased mast cell activity and elevated zonulin levels, indicating compromised gut barrier function, alongside elevated SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein expression in the terminal ileum [5]. A cross-sectional study involving 275 individuals noted marked differences in circulating myeloid and lymphocyte populations and exaggerated humoral responses against SARS-CoV-2 in those with Long COVID [27]. Chronic macrophage activation is proposed as a fundamental underlying pathophysiology [8]. Immune dysregulation can manifest as sustained activation of immune cells, T cell exhaustion, skewed B cell profiles, and disrupted immune communication, potentially leading to autoimmune complications [15][29]. Several reviews also highlight the role of autoimmunity, with evidence of *de novo* autoantibody production after SARS-CoV-2 infection, though their persistent role in causing Long COVID is debated [12][13]. A meta-analysis of RNA-seq studies identified a conserved **60-protein Long COVID Signature (LCS) score** revealing multi-compartment immune activation involving monocyte, neutrophil, and T/NK cell modules [25]. This meta-analysis also reported **unexpectedly low levels of intracellular viral RNA** in the peripheral immune system of people with Long COVID, suggesting a complex interplay where immune changes might not always directly correlate with high viral load in all compartments [10].

**Contrasting results** regarding viral persistence have been observed in some studies. While many sources support the presence of viral components [3][5][11][16][23][24][28], a case-control study from the RECOVER study found that SARS-CoV-2 viral RNA was **not detectable** in subcutaneous adipose tissue biopsies of adults with high or low symptom burden [20]. Despite this, the overall consensus from multiple reviews and studies points to both viral persistence and immune dysregulation as key, often intertwined, factors in Long COVID pathophysiology [0][1][2][4][7][13][14][17][19][21].

key_findings.text: Long COVID is characterized by persistent low-grade inflammation, T- and B-cell dysregulation, and prolonged adaptive immune activation.
Viral persistence, including the presence of SARS-CoV-2 RNA or antigens, occurs in various tissues and organs for months to years after acute infection in Long COVID patients.
The persistence of SARS-CoV-2 is hypothesized to trigger a dysregulated immune system, leading to chronic low-grade inflammation and multi-organ symptoms.
Immune dysregulation in Long COVID involves sustained activation of immune cells, T cell exhaustion, skewed B cell profiles, and disrupted immune communication.

Specific immune profiles in Long COVID patients include increased mast cell activity, elevated zonulin levels indicating compromised gut barrier function, and elevated SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein expression in the terminal ileum.
Chronic macrophage activation is proposed as a fundamental underlying pathophysiology in Long COVID.
Detection of viral RNA in recovered patients is significantly associated with the development of Long COVID symptoms, with an odds ratio of 5.17.
A meta-analysis identified a conserved 60-protein Long COVID Signature (LCS) score indicating multi-compartment immune activation.

In children and adolescents with pediatric post-COVID condition, critical hypotheses include a dysregulated immune response, persistent SARS-CoV-2 viral reservoirs, and the reactivation of latent viruses.

disagreements.issue: The detectability of SARS-CoV-2 viral RNA in specific tissues of Long COVID patients.
positions: SARS-CoV-2 viral RNA or proteins persist in various tissues such as rectosigmoid lamina propria, CD16+ monocytes, and can be detected in circulation for extended periods after acute infection [3][5][16][23][24][28].
SARS-CoV-2 viral RNA was not detectable in subcutaneous adipose tissue biopsies of adults with Long COVID [20].

disagreements.issue: The levels of intracellular viral RNA in the peripheral immune system of people with Long COVID.
positions: Many studies suggest viral persistence as a key mechanism, implying detectable viral components [3][5][11][16][23][24][28].

A meta-analysis of RNA-seq studies reported unexpectedly low levels of intracellular viral RNA in the peripheral immune system of people with Long COVID, despite significant mitochondrial transcript changes [10].

evidence_gaps: The precise mechanisms by which persistent SARS-CoV-2 RNA or antigens lead to pathogenic immune responses are not fully clear [6].
The persistence of autoantibodies and their definitive role in causing Long COVID is debated and requires further clarification [12].
The direct causal link between specific viral persistence sites and the diverse range of Long COVID symptoms is not fully elucidated.
The effectiveness of therapeutic agents targeting either viral persistence or immune dysregulation in Long COVID has not been proven [4].
